stem: Two lines on a plane surface intersect each other at a point. How many angles are formed at the point of intersection?
options: Two
Four
Three
Eight
explanation: Correct option: (B). Two intersecting lines form four angles around the point where they meet. Two angles would be seen only if we looked at one line; three is not possible; eight angles are formed when a transversal cuts two lines, not when two lines intersect.

stem: Two lines intersect and form four angles named ∠a, ∠b, ∠c and ∠d in order around the point of intersection. Which pair of angles is vertically opposite?
options: ∠a and ∠b
∠b and ∠c
∠a and ∠c
∠c and ∠d
explanation: Correct option: (C). Vertically opposite angles are the non-adjacent angles that face each other across the point, so ∠a and ∠c (and also ∠b and ∠d) are vertically opposite. The pairs ∠a and ∠b, ∠b and ∠c, and ∠c and ∠d are adjacent angles, which form linear pairs.

stem: Two lines intersect and one of the four angles is 135°. Going round the point from this angle, what are the other three angles in order?
explanation: Correct option: (D). The next angle forms a linear pair with 135°, so it is 180° - 135° = 45°. The angle after that forms a linear pair with 45°, so it is 135°, and the last one is again 45°. The order 135°, 45°, 135° puts an equal angle next to 135°, which cannot happen; 45°, 45°, 135° breaks the linear pair rule; 55° comes from a subtraction error.

stem: Reena drew two intersecting lines and measured a linear pair as 62° and 119°. What is the most likely reason that the sum is not exactly 180°?
options: Small protractor errors and thick pencil lines
Some linear pairs add up to 181° instead
Linear pairs add to 180° only when equal
The rule works only for perpendicular lines
explanation: Correct option: (A). By reasoning, a linear pair together forms a straight angle, so it always measures 180°. Measured values can differ a little because of improper use of the protractor and because drawn lines have thickness, unlike ideal lines. The rule never changes to 181°, and it holds for every pair of intersecting lines, not only equal or perpendicular angles.

stem: Two lines intersect. Three of the four angles formed add up to 250°. What is the measure of each of the two larger angles?
explanation: Correct option: (C). The four angles make two linear pairs, so together they measure 180° + 180° = 360°. The angle left out is 360° - 250° = 110°. Its linear pair is 70°, and vertically opposite angles are equal, so the angles are 110°, 70°, 110° and 70°; the larger ones are 110°. The value 70° is the smaller angle, 125° comes from halving 250°, and 140° is 250° - 110°, which mixes up the angles.

stem: Two lines intersect so that all four angles formed are equal. What is the measure of each angle?
explanation: Correct option: (A). The four angles together measure 360°, so if they are all equal each is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. Such lines are perpendicular. 45° and 60° do not add up to 360° when taken four times, and 180° is a straight angle, not an angle between two crossing lines.

stem: Which statement best describes a pair of parallel lines?
options: Lines that meet at exactly one point at 90°
Any two lines that do not meet anywhere
Two lines of equal length drawn side by side
Lines in one plane that never meet at all
explanation: Correct option: (D). Parallel lines lie on the same plane and do not meet however far they are extended at both ends. Lines meeting at 90° are perpendicular. Two lines that do not meet but lie on different planes are not called parallel, and the length of a drawn segment has nothing to do with being parallel.

stem: A line is drawn on a table top and another line is drawn on the classroom blackboard. They never meet. Are they parallel lines?

Not necessarily, as they are not on one plane
Yes, because both of them are straight lines
No, because parallel lines must be horizontal
explanation: Correct option: (B). Parallel lines must lie on the same plane and never meet. Lines on a table top and on a blackboard lie on different planes, so their never meeting does not make them parallel. Being straight is true of all lines, and parallel lines need not be horizontal.

stem: Two lines intersect and one of the four angles formed is 90°. What can be said about the other three angles?
options: Only the opposite one must be 90°
Two are 45° and one is 90°
Each of the three is also 90°
They can be found only by measuring
explanation: Correct option: (C). The angle next to 90° forms a linear pair with it, so it is 180° - 90° = 90°. The same reasoning gives 90° for the other two, so all four are right angles and the lines are perpendicular. The opposite angle is not the only one equal to 90°, 45° breaks the linear pair rule, and reasoning gives the angles without measuring.

stem: Two intersecting lines form a linear pair of angles measuring (4x - 10)° and (2x + 10)°. Are the two lines perpendicular?
options: Yes; both angles work out to 90°
No; the angles are 110° and 70°
No; the angles are 100° and 80°
Yes; x = 30 makes all angles equal
explanation: Correct option: (B). A linear pair adds up to 180°: (4x - 10) + (2x + 10) = 180, so 6x = 180 and x = 30. The angles are 4(30) - 10 = 110° and 2(30) + 10 = 70°. They are not equal, so the angles are not right angles and the lines are not perpendicular. 100° and 80° come from an arithmetic slip, and x = 30 does not make the angles equal.

They are perpendicular
They never meet

stem: A square sheet is folded horizontally in half again and again. After 1 fold there are 3 parallel horizontal lines (two edges and one crease) and after 2 folds there are 5. How many parallel lines are there after 3 folds?
explanation: Correct option: (B). The pattern is 2^n + 1 for n folds: 2 + 1 = 3, 4 + 1 = 5, and after 3 folds 8 + 1 = 9. Each new fold doubles the number of strips, so the count does not just go up by 2 (which would give 7). 8 is the number of strips, not lines, and 6 is a counting slip.

stem: In a figure, lines p and q each have one arrow mark, lines r and s each have two arrow marks, and a small square is drawn where p meets r. What does this tell us?
options: p is parallel to r, q is parallel to s, and p is perpendicular to q
p is parallel to q, r is parallel to s, and p meets r at 45°
p, q, r and s are all parallel to one another in the figure
p is parallel to q, r is parallel to s, and p is perpendicular to r
explanation: Correct option: (D). Lines with the same number of arrow marks belong to one parallel set, so p is parallel to q and r is parallel to s. The square mark shows a right angle, so p is perpendicular to r. Lines with different arrow counts are not shown as parallel, the square does not mean 45°, and the four lines cannot all be parallel when two of them meet.

stem: For repeated horizontal folds of a square sheet, the number of parallel lines after n folds is 2^n + 1. After how many folds will there be 33 parallel lines?

stem: A transversal t intersects lines l and m. A pair of corresponding angles formed is 72° and 72°. What can we conclude?

Line t is perpendicular to l
Lines l and m are parallel
Lines l and m meet to the right of t
explanation: Correct option: (C). When the corresponding angles formed by a transversal on a pair of lines are equal, the lines are parallel. Perpendicular lines meet at 90°, which is not given; t makes 72°, not 90°, with l; and parallel lines never meet on either side.

stem: A transversal t makes an angle of 110° with line l. The angle forming a linear pair with it corresponds to an angle of 75° at line m. Are l and m parallel?
options: No, as 70° and 75° are not equal
Yes, because 110° and 70° add up to 180°
Yes, as any transversal gives equal angles
No, as parallel lines need 90° angles
explanation: Correct option: (A). The linear pair of 110° is 180° - 110° = 70°. Its corresponding angle at m is 75°. Since 70° and 75° are not equal, l and m are not parallel. A linear pair always adds to 180°, so that proves nothing about l and m; a transversal gives equal corresponding angles only on parallel lines; and parallel lines need not make 90° angles with the transversal.

stem: A transversal t cuts line l and line m. Where t meets l, the four angles are ∠1 (top right), ∠2 (top left), ∠3 (bottom left) and ∠4 (bottom right); where t meets m, ∠5, ∠6, ∠7 and ∠8 are in the same positions. If ∠1 = 65° and ∠7 = 65°, what can be concluded about lines l and m?
options: l and m are perpendicular
l and m must meet
Nothing can be concluded
l and m are parallel
explanation: Correct option: (D). ∠1 and ∠3 are vertically opposite, so ∠3 = 65°. ∠3 and ∠7 are corresponding angles (both bottom left), and ∠7 = 65°, so the corresponding angles are equal and l is parallel to m. Perpendicular lines are not involved, lines with equal corresponding angles never meet, and the reasoning above does give a conclusion even though ∠1 and ∠7 are not themselves a corresponding pair.

stem: Two lines are drawn perpendicular to line l by sliding a set square along it. Which reason guarantees that the two lines are parallel?
options: They are drawn on the same side of line l
Both make 90° corresponding angles with l
They are equally long and both start on l
They meet line l at two different points
explanation: Correct option: (B). Taking l as a transversal of the two new lines, both make 90° with l, so the corresponding angles are equal and the lines are parallel. Being on the same side, being equally long or crossing l at different points does not make lines parallel; two lines crossing l at different points could still meet.

stem: To draw a line through point A parallel to line l, a set square is placed along l and a ruler is held against its other side. What is the role of the ruler?
options: It measures the distance from point A to line l
It measures the angle between the set square and l
It is used only to draw line l and is then removed
It keeps the set square from turning as it slides
explanation: Correct option: (D). The ruler is held still so that the set square can slide along it up to point A without turning. Because the set square keeps the same angle with l, the new line is parallel to l. The ruler is not used to measure the distance or the angle here, and it must stay in place while the set square slides.

Both l and m pass through the point A

stem: While drawing two lines across line l with a set square, Aman's set square slipped. One line makes 90° with l and the other makes 88° with l, in corresponding positions. What is true?
options: They are parallel as both are nearly perpendicular
They are parallel as both of them cross line l
The lines are not parallel and will meet if extended
The two lines are perpendicular to each other
explanation: Correct option: (C). Lines are parallel only when the corresponding angles are exactly equal. Here they are 90° and 88°, so the lines are not parallel and will meet if extended far enough. Being nearly perpendicular is not enough, crossing l says nothing about being parallel, and lines meeting at a small angle of 2° are not perpendicular.

stem: On a sheet, crease t is folded perpendicular to line l. Then crease m is folded through a point A on t, and crease n through another point B on t, both perpendicular to t. Which statement is true?
options: Only m and n are parallel to each other
l, m and n are all parallel to one another
m is parallel to l, but n is perpendicular to l
n is parallel to t, and m is parallel to l
explanation: Correct option: (B). Lines l, m and n each make 90° with t, so for t as a transversal every pair among them has equal corresponding angles. Hence l, m and n are all parallel. Line l is also perpendicular to t, so it belongs with m and n; n makes 90° with t, so it cannot be parallel to t or perpendicular to l.

stem: A transversal intersects a pair of parallel lines. How are a pair of alternate angles related?
options: They add up to 180°
They add up to 90°
They are equal
They are both right angles
explanation: Correct option: (C). Alternate angles formed by a transversal on parallel lines are always equal: each one equals the corresponding angle of the other, which is also vertically opposite to it. Adding up to 180° is true of interior angles on the same side, 90° has no such rule, and alternate angles are right angles only if the transversal is perpendicular.

stem: In quadrilateral ABCD, AB is parallel to DC and AD is parallel to BC. The diagonal AC is drawn. If ∠ADC = 70° and ∠DAC = 40°, what is ∠CAB?
explanation: Correct option: (B). AD is a transversal of the parallel lines AB and DC, so ∠DAB + ∠ADC = 180° (interior angles on the same side). Hence ∠DAB = 180° - 70° = 110°. Since ∠DAB = ∠DAC + ∠CAB, ∠CAB = 110° - 40° = 70°. 40° is ∠DAC itself, 110° is the whole ∠DAB, and 30° comes from 70° - 40°.

stem: AB and CD are parallel lines, AB above CD, with A and C to the left of B and D. A point O lies between the two lines, to the left of B and D, and is joined to B and D. If ∠ABO = 35° and ∠CDO = 50°, what is ∠BOD?
explanation: Correct option: (D). Draw a line through O parallel to AB (and so to CD), pointing towards B and D. With BO as a transversal, the part of ∠BOD above this line is the alternate angle of ∠ABO, so it is 35°. With DO as a transversal, the part below it is the alternate angle of ∠CDO, so it is 50°. So ∠BOD = 35° + 50° = 85°. 95° is 180° - 85°, 15° is the difference of the two angles, and 145° is 180° - 35°.
